title: Every Giant Wave Ever Measured, Shown to Scale

lines: Last August, a wave in Alaska climbed four hundred eighty-one metres up a mountain.
That is higher than the Empire State Building.
And almost nobody saw it.
It struck early in the morning, in a fjord where cruise ships carry thousands of people on summer days.
How can water rise higher than a skyscraper? Was this the tallest wave ever measured?
And could it happen again, with a ship full of people in the way?
By the end of this video, you will see every giant wave ever measured, side by side, to scale.
This is Tracy Arm, a fjord in southeast Alaska,
about one hundred thirty kilometres from the city of Juneau.
Chapter one. The empty morning.
At the end of the fjord sits the South Sawyer Glacier.
For years it had been melting back. And in early August, it suddenly retreated faster.
That ice had been holding up the mountainside above it, like a wall holding back a pile of sand.
When the ice pulled away, the slope lost its support.
The mountain gave warnings. For days, seismometers picked up tiny tremors.
In the last hours, they came every thirty to sixty seconds.
About two hours before the collapse, the tremors merged into one continuous vibration.
The slope was already sliding.
Then, on the morning of the tenth of August, the slope collapsed.
About sixty-four million cubic metres of rock fell into the water.
That is a cube of rock about four hundred metres on each side,
dropped into the fjord like a giant stone thrown into a bathtub.
Computer models show a breaking wave about one hundred metres tall,
racing at more than two hundred forty kilometres per hour.
That is roughly as tall as a thirty-storey building, moving twice as fast as a car on a motorway.
That first wave alone was taller than the Statue of Liberty.
When it hit the far side of the fjord, the water kept climbing up the mountain.
Scientists call this the run-up: the highest point the water reaches on land.
Here, it climbed to four hundred eighty-one metres, stripping the forest off the slope.
You can still see the line where the trees end.
Put the Statue of Liberty, the Eiffel Tower and the Empire State Building side by side.
The water went higher than all three.
Kayakers camping near the mouth of the fjord had their gear swept away.
Even far away in Juneau, the sea level jumped by thirty-six centimetres.
On a typical summer day, more than twenty boats, including large cruise ships, sail these fjords.
That morning, by luck, none was in Tracy Arm.
Several cruise lines have since changed their routes to avoid the area.
So far: a melting glacier let a mountain fall into a fjord, and the water climbed four hundred eighty-one metres.
But why don't ocean tsunamis get this tall?
Chapter two. Not a normal tsunami.
Most people picture a tsunami as a wave that crosses a whole ocean after an earthquake.
Those waves are fast and powerful, but much lower.
For scale, the biggest wave ever surfed was about twenty-six metres, off Nazaré in Portugal.
The highest run-up of the great tsunami in Japan, in twenty eleven, was about forty metres.
A huge disaster, but still far below Tracy Arm.
Forty metres is less than half the height of the Statue of Liberty.
Fjord waves are different. They start with one gigantic splash in deep, narrow water.
The energy has almost nowhere to spread, so the water surges up the opposite wall.
Think of dropping a brick into a bathtub. The splash hits the side and climbs the wall.
Now make the brick a piece of a mountain.
So the tallest waves on Earth don't happen on open ocean coasts.
They happen in quiet, narrow fjords.
So far: the tallest waves are splash waves in fjords, not ocean tsunamis.
And Tracy Arm is not the only one.
Chapter three. The ladder of giants.
Twenty fifteen. Taan Fiord, Alaska.
A slope weakened by a shrinking glacier slid into the water, with nobody watching.
Scientists only found out from seismometers and satellite photos.
The water had climbed one hundred ninety-three metres.
That is about twice the height of the Statue of Liberty.
Twenty twenty-three. Dickson Fjord, in eastern Greenland.
Twenty-five million cubic metres of rock and ice crashed into the water.
The wave reached about two hundred metres. Then something stranger happened.
The water kept sloshing from side to side, like water in a bathtub.
For nine days, seismometers all over the world recorded a strange, regular signal.
Nobody knew what it was, until scientists traced it to this fjord.
Nineteen eighty. When Mount Saint Helens erupted, a huge landslide crashed into Spirit Lake.
The water surged about two hundred sixty-five metres up the hills.
All of these are enormous. But none of them reaches the top of the Eiffel Tower.
Only two waves in recorded history have gone higher.
So far: Taan Fiord, Greenland and Spirit Lake all passed one hundred ninety metres.
So which wave holds the record?
Chapter four. The record.
Nineteen fifty-eight. Lituya Bay, another narrow bay on the coast of Alaska.
A powerful earthquake shook loose about thirty million cubic metres of rock,
which fell from high above the water.
That evening, Howard Ulrich and his seven-year-old son were anchored in their fishing boat, the Edrie.
They saw a wall of water rushing toward them. The boat was lifted onto the wave.
And somehow, both of them survived.
Ulrich later estimated that the wave passing his boat was up to thirty metres high, and that was out in the middle of the bay.
Afterwards, geologist Don Miller measured the line where the forest had been torn away.
It reached five hundred twenty-four metres.
Along that line, trees were ripped out by their roots or stripped of their bark.
Higher than the Empire State Building. Higher than Tracy Arm.
It is the tallest wave run-up ever recorded.
So far: the record is Lituya Bay, five hundred twenty-four metres, and Tracy Arm is second.
So will there be more?
Chapter five. Why there will be more.
All these giants share one cause: steep slopes falling into deep water.
And in Alaska and Greenland, melting glaciers are uncovering more of those slopes.
A study of Glacier Bay in Alaska found that rock avalanches there have been getting bigger in recent decades.
In Greenland, scientists linked the Dickson Fjord slide to a glacier below it that had been thinning for decades.
Right now, scientists are watching a slope above Barry Arm, in Prince William Sound.
It is creeping slowly toward the water.
If it fell all at once, models warn of waves over two hundred metres near the slide,
reaching the town of Whittier in about twenty minutes.
The good news: Tracy Arm showed that these mountains can warn us first.
Scientists say Alaska now needs to watch its slopes the way it already watches earthquakes and volcanoes.
So far: shrinking glaciers mean more falling slopes, and more giant waves.
Now, let's put every giant side by side.
Chapter six. Every giant wave, to scale.
Taan Fiord, one hundred ninety-three metres. Greenland, about two hundred.
Spirit Lake, two hundred sixty-five.
Tracy Arm, four hundred eighty-one.
And the record, Lituya Bay, five hundred twenty-four metres.
For comparison: the Statue of Liberty is ninety-three metres tall.
The Empire State Building reaches four hundred forty-three to the tip.
And even the record is less than two thirds of the Burj Khalifa, the tallest building on Earth.
So what would it take to send water to the top of the Burj?
Nobody knows. And let's hope we never find out.
So here is my question: knowing all this, would you still take a cruise into an Alaskan fjord?
Tell me in the comments.
